name: Shendu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: No Shendu-specific description found; closest is Savidge 1908, A Grammar and Dictionary of the Lakher Language (archive.org, read — covers related Mara/Lakher, note: final long vowels 'not as a rule accented'), not Shendu proper

tone_statements.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2023. Tone in South Central Tibeto-Burman. Himalayan Linguistics 22(1): 35-66. doi:10.5070/H922153559
tone_statements.quote: Some languages reportedly have only one Falling contour, as in Mara, E. Hyow, and Zotung.13 [...] 12 The tone inventories of Maraic languages are often described as involving three pitch (and in some cases tone) levels. In addition to Senthang, Zophei and Mara are also reported to use three pitch levels, along with contours. Mara makes a lexical contrast between L, M, and H morphemes, with a HM Fall occurring in derived environments (Arden 2010: 49-50, 65).
tone_statements.locator: p. 40 (running text 'only one Falling contour, as in Mara..' and footnote 12); Table 1 inventory row for Mara p. 39; Savidge remark p. 37

tone_statements.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2021. The Sound Systems of Zophei Dialects and Other Maraic Languages. PhD dissertation, Indiana University. 437 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Arden (2010) (though not Löffler, 2002 nor Van Bik, 2009) describes vowel contrasts in terms of lowering /i i̞ ɑ ɑ̞ u u̞/, as well as 3 tone levels: High, Mid, and Low. Löffler (2002) also speaks to the central importance of indicating 3 tone levels in the orthography, noting that written Mara is too ambiguous to be functional without tone marks. [...] In addition to Senthang, Zophei and Mara are also reported to use three pitch levels, along with contours. Mara makes a lexical contrast between L, M, and H morphemes, with a HM Fall occurring in derived environments (Arden, 2010, pp. 49-50, 65).
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 level (H, M, L) + derived HM fall

tone_statements.citation: Arden, Michelle J. 2010. A phonetic, phonological, and morphosyntactic analysis of the Mara language. MA thesis, San Jose State University (Master's Theses 3744). doi:10.31979/etd.v36r-dk3u. 105 pp. (Glottolog: 179 pp., listed by Glottolog as a grammar, listed under mara1382)
tone_statements.quote: The Mara language is primarily a three-tone system, although some exceptions exist. Our speaker characterized the tones as a low-mid-high “do-re-mi” scale. … There is ample evidence that all three tones are contrastive. Despite the prevalence of this three-tone system, some exceptions were found with high-mid contour tones together with what seems to be an unusually long vowel. … The falling tone in Mara is regular but rare in lexical contexts. More commonly, it appears in morphologically derived contexts.
tone_statements.locator: 5.3 Three-tone System, p. 49 and 6.3.1 Falling contour tones, p. 65

tone_statements.citation: VanBik, Kenneth. 2009. Proto-Kuki-Chin: A Reconstructed Ancestor of the Kuki-Chin Languages. STEDT Monograph Series 8. Berkeley: STEDT, University of California. xxiv+626 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Because of that, Mara tones are marked with numbers (L as 1, M as 2, and H as 3), rather than with diacritical marks. [...] For smooth syllables, F. Lai37 and Mizo38 have four tones (High, Falling, Rising, and Low), H. Lai39 has three tones (Falling, Rising, Low), Tedim has three tones marked numerically as (1, 2, 3)40, and Thado Kuki41 has three (High, Falling, Low). Note that the underlying High tone of Thado Kuki is realized as Rising in isolation (Hyman 2004). Mara has three tones (High, Mid, Low).
tone_statements.locator: p. 375 (§5.1.2.3.13, tone-numbering remark) and p. 452 (§6.1.1 Smooth Syllables, 'Mara has three tones (High, Mid, Low)', with Table 162 on the same page); Luce/Khoi discussion p. 451
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page for shen1247 (Shendu) and ISO 639-3 registry page for shl / change request 2025-055 (read online 2026-09-17)
sources.note: Identity only. Glottolog: 'Shendu is but a colonial-time appellation for the Mara Chin' [mrh]; no descriptive references listed (n=0); cites Lewin 1869, Tickell 1852, Hughes 1881 as name sources. ISO 639-3 CR 2025-055 (adopted, effective 2026-07-15): shl retired as a duplicate, replaced by mrh (Mara), 'Shendu' added as a name of mrh.

sources.citation: Löffler, Lorenz G. 2004. Some notes on Maraa: II. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 27(1): 61-87. doi:10.15144/LTBA-27.1.61 (also 10.32655/ltba.27.1.03, hdl 10356/177976)
sources.note: Dialect comparison (Tlongsai vs Sabeu), tones and sandhi contours, prefixes, reconstruction. No occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' at all (re-a full-text search for stress/accent today).

sources.citation: Löffler, Lorenz G. 2002. Some notes on Maraa. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25(1): 123-136. doi:10.15144/LTBA-25.1.123 (also 10.32655/ltba.25.1.05, hdl 10356/178032)
sources.note: §2 'Phonemes and tones' (pp. 124-127): three tones (low, high, mid); Savidge and Lorrain 'failed to recognize the importance of tones'; Lorrain's few lines on tones (his p. 59) 'mostly wrong'. The only 'stress' mentions are vowel-internal: diphthong /ie/ 'with the stress on the second vowel; a Frenchman would have written it /ié/' (p. 126) and 'MM /ie/ (with the stress on a very narrow [e])' (p. 133). No word-stress statement (re-a full-text search for stress/accent today).

sources.citation: Lorrain, Reginald Arthur. 1951. Grammar and dictionary of the Lakher or Mara language. Gauhati: Government of Assam, Dept. of Historical and Antiquarian Studies. x+372 pp. — ONLY the 3 Rosetta Project pages (title, introduction, Part I Orthography)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, HathiTrust search-only; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 1286.180)
sources.note: Orthography only: 'there are only a very few instances where the vowel needs a circumflex accent placed over it to increase the length of that sound.. forgetting to accent such a vowel or vice versa changes the meaning entirely' — 'accent' = length diacritic, not stress. Full grammar (pp. 1-59, tone note reported by Löffler at p. 59) not open: HathiTrust record 000756017 is search-only per catalog page returned a block page by automated download today); Harvard print Widener Library 1286.180.

tone.quote: The Mara language is primarily a three-tone system, although some exceptions exist. Our speaker characterized the tones as a low-mid-high “do-re-mi” scale. … There is ample evidence that all three tones are contrastive. Despite the prevalence of this three-tone system, some exceptions were found with high-mid contour tones together with what seems to be an unusually long vowel. … The falling tone in Mara is regular but rare in lexical contexts. tone.locator: 5.3 Three-tone System, p. 49 and 6.3.1 Falling contour tones, p. 65
tone.says: Three contrastive level tones, low, mid and high; a high-mid falling contour is rare in the lexicon and mostly arises in derived contexts (possessives, demonstratives, clitics). Silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Parry, N. E. 1932. The Lakhers. London: Macmillan (appendix with dialect vocabulary and notes on the language)
sources.note: Ethnography with a linguistic appendix comparing Mara dialects; the only other early primary source; stress remark unlikely but unchecked.

sources.citation: Savidge, Fred W. 1908. A grammar and dictionary of the Lakher language. Allahabad: Pioneer Press. 225 pp.
sources.note: 'Lakher alphabet and pronunciation' pp. 1-2 only. Footnote to the circumflexed long vowels: '* The final vowels of words and syllables being generally long, they are not as a rule accented.' — 'accented' = carrying the circumflex length mark (orthography), not word stress. No stress description; tones not recognised.

sources.citation: Tickell, S. R. 1852. Notes on the Heumá or "Shendoos," a tribe inhabiting the hills north of Arracan. Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 21: 207-243. (Glottolog ref 303875, wordlist, 'Shendoos = Shendu = Mara Chin [mrh]')
sources.note: Only Shendu-proper primary source. Vocabulary preface (pp. 212-213) says just 'The dialect is exceedingly guttural, gh being exactly rendered by the Arabic [ghain] and kh by the Persian [khe] while in their vowel sounds éw and ü have precisely the sounds of the French vowels in deux, and u in flute'. Nothing on accent, stress or tone (a full-text search for stress/accent|pronunc|tone|syllab over the paper: no hits). Wordlist + sentences follow.
